hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there a place you’d love to go back to, because something important started there?
options: then you’ll understand this emperor. listen.
places hold people, don’t they? listen.
then let me take you to one that millions visit.

steps.line: A century or two after the Buddha, India had a great emperor, Ashoka. After a terrible war, he was filled with regret, and turned to the Buddha’s teaching.
Years later, he traveled in person to a small garden called Lumbini, the place where the Buddha had been born.

steps.q: He wants this spot never to be forgotten. What do you think he does?
o: Builds a great stupa over the spot
Sets up a carved stone pillar
Gives the land to the monks
steps.why: A pillar, and it’s still standing. Ashoka set up pillars across his empire, but this one names the exact spot.

steps.line: He bowed there, and had a tall stone pillar set up. Carved on it, in plain words: here the Buddha, the sage of the Sakyas, was born.

steps.q: The carving calls the Buddha “the sage of the Sakyas.” Who were the Sakyas?
o: The clan he was born into
The kings who ruled before Ashoka
steps.why: His own people, in the foothills where Lumbini lies. That’s why Buddhists call him Sakyamuni, the sage of the Sakyas.

steps.line: He also freed the village of Lumbini from most of its taxes. It would pay only an eighth share of its harvest. A gift, for the place he was born.

steps.q: Why lighten the taxes of the village around the garden?
o: To pay the villagers for the land
To reward them for keeping the spot
To honor the birthplace through its people
steps.why: The carving gives the reason in so many words: because the Buddha was born here. Honoring a holy place meant easing life for the people beside it.

steps.line: Over the centuries, the jungle grew back and the place was nearly forgotten. In 1896, the pillar was found again, its words still readable.

steps.q: Long before 1896, a Chinese monk, Xuanzang, walked to Lumbini and wrote about a pillar there, split by lightning. Why did his diary matter?
o: It proved the Buddha was born there
It told searchers what to look for, and where
It gave the exact words on the pillar
steps.why: Pilgrim diaries from China, by Faxian and later Xuanzang, guided searchers to many Buddhist sites lost under the jungle.

steps.line: Today, pilgrims from Sri Lanka, Thailand, Tibet, Japan and far beyond walk through Lumbini’s gardens, past Ashoka’s pillar, to the place he was born.
steps.label: today

say: lumbini is one of four places the buddha himself is remembered naming for pilgrims: where he was born, where he woke up, where he first taught, and where he died. go, he said, and be moved.

every school treats lumbini as shared ground, and around the garden stand monasteries built by theravada, mahayana and tibetan buddhists side by side. the pillar matters to historians too: stone evidence that people already honored this spot long ago.

steps.q: Why does Ashoka’s pillar matter even to historians who don’t share the faith?
o: It records the Buddha’s birth date
It proves the birth story’s wonders
It shows the spot was honored by 250 BCE
steps.why: It can’t prove the wonders, or even a date. It does show that within a few centuries the birthplace was remembered, and carved in stone.

today.say: today, think of a place where something good began for you: a school, a kitchen, a hospital, a friend’s porch. go back sometime if you can, or just picture it, and give thanks there. that’s pilgrimage, small size.
options: then go there in your mind, for one breath.
maybe one day. the garden will wait.

sources: Lumbini (Rummindei) pillar inscription of Ashoka: twenty years after his consecration he came in person and worshipped; “here the Buddha, the sage of the Sakyas, was born”; a stone pillar set up; the village of Lumbini made free of tax (ubalike) and paying an eighth share (athabhagiye)
Ashoka’s Rock Edict XIII: his remorse after the conquest of Kalinga
Mahaparinibbana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 16, 5.8): the four places worth seeing for a faithful follower
Rediscovery of the pillar in December 1896 (Khadga Shumsher Rana and Alois Anton Führer); Lumbini as a UNESCO World Heritage Site; the international monastic zone
check: Dates for Ashoka relative to the Buddha vary by scholar; “a century or two after” follows the day script.
The reading of “eighth share” and “free of tax” follows the usual translation of the inscription.
The pillar no longer has its original top; the keepsake drawing is a simple pillar.
